q: What does the case of the widow in paragraph 3 of the cholera passage suggest?
o: She caught cholera during an earlier visit to Soho.
Cholera could spread through the air over long distances.
Wells in her own district were also contaminated.
The pump's water, not Soho's air, carried the disease.
w: She lived miles away, so she did not breathe Soho's air, yet she died after drinking Broad Street water. Her case points to the water, which is why the author lists it among the revealing exceptions.

n.0: Unsupported: the passage links her illness to water carried to her home, and mentions no visit.
n.1: Opposite: her case argues against airborne miasma.
n.2: Unsupported, and it would weaken the point: she drank Broad Street water by preference.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by paragraph 4 of the cholera passage?
o: Removing the pump handle brought the outbreak to an end within a single day.
Removing the handle may have helped but does not fully explain the drop in deaths.
Residents fled Soho because officials had closed the public pump on Broad Street.
Local officials accepted the miasma theory after hearing Snow's report.
w: Deaths fell after the handle came off, but Snow admitted the outbreak was already slowing and many residents had fled. The modest conclusion respects both facts.

n.0: Overstatement: deaths 'fell soon afterward', and the outbreak was already slowing.
n.2: Reversed sequence: residents had fled before the handle was removed, which helped slow the outbreak.
n.3: Unsupported: officials acted on Snow's evidence; paragraph 5 says his explanation was not widely accepted at first.

q: What can be inferred from paragraph 5 of the passage about respiratory therapists?
o: Most therapists now hold a bachelor's degree or higher.
Newborn care pays more than other specialties in the field.
An associate degree no longer qualifies a person to practice.
The field offers room to advance beyond the entry-level degree.
w: An associate degree is the minimum, and many therapists 'later earn a bachelor's degree or specialize', which implies paths for advancement after entry.

n.0: Overstatement: 'many' later earn one; that does not mean most hold one.
n.1: Unsupported: the passage says nothing about pay.
n.2: Contradiction: the passage says an associate degree is the minimum requirement.

q: Why does the author mention the child with asthma in paragraph 4 of the passage about respiratory therapists?
o: To illustrate the teaching part of a therapist's work
To show that asthma is the most common lung disease in children
To contrast the care of children with the care of adults
To explain how a spacer changes the dose from an inhaler
w: Paragraph 4 opens 'Teaching is a quieter but equally important part of the job'; the child learning to use a spacer is an example of that teaching.

n.1: Unsupported: the passage never ranks childhood lung diseases.
n.2: Wrong relationship: the adult with COPD is a second example of teaching, not a contrast.
n.3: Not explained: the passage names the spacer but says nothing about how it works.

q: A healthy adult drinks a cup with 100 milligrams of caffeine at noon. Based on paragraph 3 of the caffeine passage, which inference is best supported?
o: All of it will be gone from the body by 10 p.m.
The person will have trouble falling asleep that night.
About half of it may still be in the body at 5 p.m.
The caffeine would clear faster if the person were pregnant.
w: With an average half-life of about five hours, roughly 50 milligrams would remain five hours later. 'May' respects the wide range between people.

n.0: Overreach: after two half-lives about a quarter would remain, as the 3 p.m. to 1 a.m. example shows.
n.1: Overreach: paragraph 4 says lingering caffeine can affect even people who fall asleep easily, so trouble falling asleep is not implied.
n.3: Reversal: paragraph 3 says pregnancy slows caffeine's breakdown.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by the sleep study described in paragraph 4 of the caffeine passage?
o: Caffeine six hours before bed keeps most people awake all night.
Caffeine can shorten sleep even when a person does not notice it.
Adults who use caffeine sleep an hour less on every night.
A placebo improves sleep more than taking no caffeine does.
w: Adults who took caffeine six hours before bed slept about an hour less on average, yet many did not notice: the modest conclusion uses both findings.

n.0: Overstatement: they slept about an hour less, not all night awake.
n.2: Overgeneralization: one laboratory study of a large dose six hours before bed, not every caffeine user on every night.
n.3: Misreading: the placebo was the comparison condition; the study did not compare it with taking nothing.

q: Based on paragraph 4 of the food safety passage, which inference about a roast thawed on the counter is best supported?
o: It is safe on the counter if it weighs under 4 pounds.
Its center warms into the danger zone before its surface.
It can be safely refrozen once it has thawed completely.
It may be unsafe even while part of it is still frozen.
w: The outside 'can warm into the danger zone while its center is still icy', so a partly frozen roast can still have a surface where bacteria multiply.

n.0: Overreach: the 4 to 5 pound figure is the refrigerator thawing rate, not a safe size for counter thawing.
n.1: Reversal: the outside warms first while the center stays icy.
n.2: Outside knowledge: the passage says nothing about refreezing.

q: Which conclusion about home food safety is best supported by the passage?
o: Most foodborne illness in the United States begins in home kitchens.
Controlling time and temperature at home lowers the risk of foodborne illness.
Food that still smells normal is safe to eat after sitting out overnight.
Microwave thawing is the safest of the three methods the USDA lists.
w: Every paragraph turns on time and temperature: the danger zone and the two-hour rule, quick cooling, safe thawing and cooking temperatures.

n.0: Overgeneralization: the passage says only that not every case begins in a restaurant.
n.2: Contradiction: food in the danger zone 'may look and smell normal' and still make someone sick.
n.3: Unsupported: the three methods are all called safe, and none is ranked safest.

q: Which statement from the passage on food safety expresses an opinion?
o: Within it, many bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes.
Planning a meal a day ahead is a small price to pay for that peace of mind.
Poultry is safe to eat once it reaches an internal temperature of 165°F.
The refrigerator method is the slowest, needing about a day for every 4 to 5 pounds of food.
w: 'A small price to pay' is a value judgment: whether the planning is worth it cannot be proven, and readers could disagree.

n.0: Fact: a measurable claim that can be checked by laboratory evidence.
n.2: Fact: a published safety standard that can be verified.
n.3: Fact: thawing times can be measured and compared.

q: What is the main idea of the passage on hands-only CPR?
o: Every state protects bystanders who help in an emergency by law.
Most people who have a cardiac arrest outside a hospital die.
Adults should learn hands-only CPR, a simple skill that saves lives.
Schools should teach every student basic emergency medicine.
w: The author argues throughout that more people should learn hands-only CPR: the need (1), the simplicity and benefit (2), answers to objections (3), how easy learning is (4) and a call to act (5).

n.0: Too narrow: Good Samaritan laws are one answer to an objection in paragraph 3.
n.1: Too narrow: this statistic sets up the problem; it is not the author's point.
n.3: Distortion and too broad: the author backs a CPR graduation rule, not emergency medicine courses.

q: Based on the passage on hands-only CPR, what can be inferred about a bystander who performs it?
o: The bystander needs a CPR card to be protected by law.
The bystander should add a rescue breath every minute.
The bystander can help without formal medical training.
The bystander can usually restart the heart without help.
w: The two steps need no breaths, free videos teach the technique in minutes, and the law protects 'reasonable help': together these imply an untrained person can help.

n.0: Unsupported: Good Samaritan laws cover people who give reasonable help; no card is mentioned.
n.1: Contradiction: 'No rescue breaths are needed.'
n.3: Overreach: compressions keep blood moving until paramedics or a defibrillator restore the rhythm.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage on hands-only CPR?
o: Bystander CPR saves most people who have a cardiac arrest.
Fear of lawsuits is the main reason most bystanders hesitate.
Hands-only CPR works as well as a defibrillator in an arrest.
Wider CPR training could raise survival from cardiac arrest.
w: Many bystanders do not act because they do not know how, and prompt bystander CPR can double or triple survival: more trained people should mean more survivors.

n.0: Overstatement: doubling or tripling a low survival rate does not make it most people.
n.1: Distortion: paragraph 1 gives not knowing what to do as the reason; fear of being sued is one worry in paragraph 3.
n.2: Unsupported: CPR keeps blood moving until a defibrillator can restore a normal rhythm.

q: What is the author's primary purpose in the passage on hands-only CPR?
o: To persuade readers to learn and use hands-only CPR
To explain how hands-only CPR differs from CPR with breaths
To inform readers about the causes of cardiac arrest
To criticize bystanders who fail to help in emergencies
w: The passage makes a claim, answers objections, uses 'should' and ends with a call to action: the purpose is to persuade.

n.1: Inform trap: the passage notes no rescue breaths are needed, but uses that fact to persuade.
n.2: Off target: the passage defines cardiac arrest but never discusses its causes.
n.3: Wrong attitude: the author says bystanders hold back because they do not know what to do, not because they do not care.

q: Which statement from the passage on hands-only CPR is a fact?
o: Employers, too, should offer training to every worker.
Many states now require high school students to learn CPR.
These worries are understandable, but they are misplaced.
The skill they need is simpler than most people think.
w: Graduation requirements can be checked in state law, so this is verifiable.

n.0: Opinion: 'should' signals a recommendation others could reject.
n.2: Opinion: 'understandable' and 'misplaced' are the author's judgments.
n.3: Opinion: a judgment about difficulty and about what most people think, not a verifiable fact.

q: What can be inferred about why Mr. Halvorsen pushed away his dinner tray in the story about Room 412?
o: He disliked the food that the hospital served.
He was grieving and had lost his appetite.
He wanted Lena to stay and talk with him.
He had trouble cutting his food without help.
w: His wife used to cut his meat, his hands are stiff, and once his food arrived precut he ate nearly everything: the evidence points to difficulty cutting.

n.0: Unsupported: he ate nearly everything once it was cut, so taste was not the problem.
n.1: Possible but outweighed: he grieves, yet he ate well the next evening once the food was precut.
n.2: Overreach: he did talk the next evening, but nothing shows he refused food to get company.

q: Why does the author include paragraph 5 in the story about Room 412?
o: To explain how Lena became a registered nurse
To describe how assistants record vital signs
To show the lesson Lena carried into her career
To show that Mr. Halvorsen recovered fully
w: Paragraph 5 jumps to Lena as a trainer passing on what Room 412 taught her: records show what, not why, so ask.

n.0: Distortion: the paragraph mentions her role but not how she reached it.
n.1: Off target: vital signs appear in paragraph 1; paragraph 5 is about asking why.
n.3: Unsupported: the story never says whether he recovered.

q: According to the sodium passage, why do the kidneys hold on to extra water after a person eats more sodium than the body needs?
o: To dilute the extra sodium in the body
To lower the volume of blood in the vessels
To replace water lost in salty sweat
To ease the pressure on the vessel walls
w: Paragraph 3 states that the kidneys 'hold on to extra water to dilute it,' meaning the extra sodium.

n.1: Reversal: holding water raises blood volume; the passage says the added fluid increases the volume moving through the vessels.
n.2: Sweat is not mentioned; this answer depends on outside ideas, not the passage.
n.3: Reversal: the higher volume pushes harder against the vessel walls, so pressure rises rather than eases.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by the figures in paragraphs 1 and 2 of the sodium passage?
o: Bread supplies most of the sodium in the average American diet.
The average adult eats about twice the advised daily sodium limit.
Restaurant meals supply more sodium than packaged foods for most adults.
Someone who adds no salt at the table can still eat more than the limit.
w: The average intake is about 3,400 mg against a 2,300 mg limit, and more than 70 percent of sodium is in food before it reaches the table. Seventy percent of 3,400 mg is about 2,380 mg, already above the limit, so a person who adds no salt can still exceed it.

n.0: Overstatement: bread is listed among the largest sources, and a slice holds 100 to 200 mg; the passage does not say bread supplies most sodium.
n.1: Number slip: 3,400 mg is nearly 50 percent more than 2,300 mg, not twice as much (twice would be 4,600 mg).
n.2: The 70 percent figure groups processing and restaurant cooking together; the passage does not compare the two sources.

q: Which statement from the sodium passage expresses an opinion rather than a fact?
o: The average American adult eats about 3,400 milligrams a day, nearly 50 percent more than that limit.
Reading the Nutrition Facts label is one of the most practical tools a shopper has.
The label lists sodium in milligrams per serving and as a percent Daily Value.
Bread, deli meats, pizza, canned soups and packaged snacks are among the largest sources.
w: 'One of the most practical tools' is a judgment about usefulness that reasonable people could dispute; it cannot be measured or checked the way an amount or a label's contents can.

n.0: An average intake can be checked against diet surveys; the figure makes the statement measurable, and it contains no judgment.
n.2: What a label lists can be verified by looking at any Nutrition Facts label.
n.3: Which foods supply the most sodium can be checked against diet studies; 'largest' here is a measurable amount, not a judgment.

q: What does paragraph 4 of the antibiotic passage imply by saying that "most sore throats" are caused by viruses?
o: Antibiotics can kill the viruses behind most sore throats.
Sore throats are the most common reason for antibiotic prescriptions.
Not every sore throat is caused by a virus.
Sore throats caused by bacteria cannot be treated with antibiotics.
w: 'Most' is a qualifier: if most sore throats are viral, some are not. The passage implies this without stating it, which is why antibiotics are not useful for most sore throats but can be for others.

n.0: Contradicts paragraph 4, which says viruses are something 'antibiotics cannot kill.'
n.1: Unsupported: the passage gives no ranking of the reasons antibiotics are prescribed.
n.3: Reversal: paragraph 4 says 'Antibiotics work against bacteria'; it is viral illnesses they cannot treat.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by paragraphs 2 and 4 of the antibiotic passage?
o: Cutting unneeded prescriptions should give resistant bacteria fewer chances to take over.
Antibiotics given for the flu make the flu virus itself resistant to those antibiotics.
Most antibiotic prescriptions written in doctors' offices and clinics are not needed.
Resistance genes stay inside the one kind of bacteria in which they first appear.
w: Paragraph 2 explains that each use of an antibiotic lets resistant bacteria survive and multiply, and paragraph 4 says many prescriptions are unneeded and expose bacteria to the drug for no benefit. Fewer unneeded prescriptions should mean fewer such chances.

n.1: Reversal of the mechanism: antibiotics cannot kill viruses, and the passage describes resistance in bacteria, not in the flu virus.
n.2: Number misread: 'at least 28 percent' is not 'most'; the figure does not support a majority.
n.3: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says bacteria can pass resistance genes to one another.

q: Which statement can be inferred from paragraph 5 of the fever passage?
o: Fever-reducing medicines do more harm than good in healthy adults.
Infants usually develop higher fevers than older adults do.
A moderate fever calls for prompt care in most healthy adults.
The same fever may call for different responses in different people.
w: Paragraph 5 says infants, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may need prompt care even for a moderate fever, while a mild fever in a healthy adult is usually a clue that the body is fighting back. Together these imply that the right response depends partly on who has the fever.

n.0: Contradicts the paragraph, which says many doctors recommend these medicines for comfort.
n.1: The paragraph says infants may need prompt care, not that their fevers run higher; that idea needs outside knowledge.
n.2: Overgeneralization: prompt care for a moderate fever is linked to infants, older adults and people with weakened immunity, not to most healthy adults.

q: What is the author's primary purpose in the passage about fever?
o: To explain how and why the body raises its temperature in infection
To persuade readers to stop taking medicine that lowers a fever
To describe one patient's experience of a high fever and recovery
To warn readers that high fevers often cause lasting harm to health
w: The passage explains the mechanism (set point, shivering, sweating) and the reasons (slowing germs, speeding white blood cells) in neutral language. Its purpose is to inform.

n.1: The passage says many doctors recommend these medicines for comfort; it does not argue against them.
n.2: No individual patient appears; the passage describes fever in general terms.
n.3: Paragraph 5 notes that very high temperatures can be dangerous, but one caution is not the purpose of the whole passage, and 'often cause lasting harm' overstates it.

q: Which statement can be inferred from paragraph 4 of the vaccine passage?
o: Each health problem reported to VAERS was caused by a vaccine.
The FDA licenses most of the vaccines that complete Phase 3.
Some side effects are too rare to show up even in large trials.
Outside experts make the final decision on licensing a vaccine.
w: Paragraph 4 says monitoring after approval allows 'rare side effects that did not appear in trials to be detected.' If some effects appear only after approval, trials of thousands of people can miss very rare ones.

n.0: Overreach: VAERS collects reports of problems after vaccination; the passage does not say every reported problem was caused by the vaccine.
n.1: Possible but unsupported: the passage gives no approval rates.
n.3: Distortion: the FDA often consults outside experts, but the agency decides whether to license.

q: Based on paragraph 3 of the vaccine passage, which conclusion is best supported?
o: Volunteers who receive the placebo are protected from the disease.
Results could be less trustworthy if researchers knew who got the vaccine.
Phase 3 is the most important of the three phases of clinical trials.
A vaccine that completes Phase 2 is likely to be licensed by the FDA.
w: The paragraph explains that neither volunteers nor researchers know who received which shot, so their expectations cannot affect the results. It follows that if they did know, expectations could bias the findings.

n.0: Contradicts the passage: a placebo has no active ingredient, and comparing illness in the two groups works because the placebo group is not protected.
n.2: Paragraph 3 calls Phase 3 the largest stage; largest does not mean most important.
n.3: The passage gives no approval odds and notes that a vaccine can be stopped at any stage.

q: Which sentence from the drinking fountain passage best states its main idea?
o: Many were shut off during the COVID-19 pandemic and have stayed off since.
Families with money can carry bottled water or buy a drink at the snack bar.
Every public park and school should have a working water station.
When water is free and easy to reach, people drink more of it.
w: Paragraph 1 states the claim that the rest of the passage supports: health, cost, cleanliness and fairness are all reasons for working water stations, and paragraph 6 asks readers to push for exactly that.

n.0: Background detail from paragraph 1 that sets up the problem; it is not the point the author argues.
n.1: A supporting detail for the fairness reason in paragraph 5.
n.3: A supporting detail for the health reason in paragraph 2.

q: What does the author of the drinking fountain passage suggest by comparing the cost of a water station with the cost of playground upgrades?
o: The council has already voted down a plan for new water stations.
The council could afford water stations if it chose to fund them.
Playground upgrades are a waste of the parks budget each year.
The council cares little about the health of the city's children.
w: A station costs 'far less than many of the playground upgrades councils approve without debate.' The comparison implies that money is not the real obstacle: the council already pays for costlier projects.

n.0: Unsupported: the passage says the council will vote in March; it mentions no earlier rejection.
n.2: Overreach: the author compares costs but does not call playground upgrades wasteful.
n.3: Overreach: the author questions a funding choice and treats the council's cleanliness concern with respect; the passage does not say members care little about children.

q: Why does the author of the drinking fountain passage most likely include paragraph 4?
o: To explain how filters remove germs from drinking water
To compare the cost of new stations with old fountains
To describe the condition of fountains in local parks
To answer an objection that opponents might raise
w: Paragraph 4 opens with council members' worry about cleanliness and then answers it (no mouth contact with the spout, scheduled filter changes, regular cleaning). Raising and answering an opposing concern is a persuasive move.

n.0: Filters are mentioned as one feature, but the paragraph does not explain how they work; its job is to answer a worry.
n.1: Costs are discussed in paragraph 3; paragraph 4 is about cleanliness.
n.2: The condition of local fountains is described in paragraph 1.

q: Which statement from the drinking fountain passage is a fact rather than an opinion?
o: That is a mistake our communities can no longer afford.
Some council members worry about cleanliness, and that concern deserves a real answer.
One study found that middle school students drank more water after new filling stations were installed.
Children whose families cannot afford bottled water should not have to choose between thirst and soda.
w: A study's reported finding can be checked against the study itself. The sentence reports what was found and adds no judgment.

n.0: Calling the closures 'a mistake' is a judgment others could dispute.
n.1: Mixed sentence: council members' worry is checkable, but 'that concern deserves a real answer' is a judgment, so the sentence contains an opinion.
n.3: 'Should not have to' expresses a value judgment about what is right, which cannot be proven.

q: What is the main idea of the passage about the glucose meter?
o: Older adults find glucose meters hard to learn to use at home.
The father managed his diabetes once he could do it his own way.
The narrator chose a nursing career because of the father's illness.
Charts are the most effective way to teach patients about diabetes.
w: The story moves from the father's refusal, through the chart that let him begin on his own terms, to his ownership of his numbers, and the last paragraph says he needed a way to take charge that felt like his own idea.

n.0: Unsupported generalization: the nurse had shown him how to use the meter; his problem was willingness, not difficulty.
n.2: Unsupported: the narrator was already taking nursing prerequisites; the passage does not say the illness caused that choice.
n.3: Overgeneralization: the narrator says, 'I have since learned many better ways to teach patients.'

q: Why does the narrator of the glucose meter passage most likely record a blood pressure reading on the chart each morning?
o: To model the habit without telling the father what to do
Because an anatomy course required daily blood pressure records
To show the father that the narrator's numbers were worse than his
Because the nurse had asked the family to track readings together
w: Paragraph 3 says the narrator 'didn't lecture' and recorded the readings 'where he could see them,' as part of an approach the father would respect. The clues point to setting an example rather than giving orders.

n.1: Possible but unsupported: the cuff came from an anatomy kit, but the passage does not say the course required daily records.
n.2: Unsupported: the narrator's numbers are not compared with the father's anywhere in the passage.
n.3: Unsupported: the nurse is described teaching the father to use the meter, not asking the family to track readings.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage about the glucose meter?
o: The chart cured the father's diabetes within three months.
The nurse's warnings were what finally changed the father's mind.
The chart, not his diet, caused the father's improved results.
The father came to treat his readings as something he could manage.
w: Paragraph 5 shows him starting his own chart, adding a food column and talking about what makes his numbers 'run rough' or 'run smooth,' like engines he could fix. He came to see his readings as something he could understand and manage.

n.0: Overstatement: the nurse said his results had improved; the passage does not say his diabetes was cured.
n.1: Unsupported: no warnings from the nurse are described; the change follows the chart on the refrigerator.
n.2: Causal overreach: he also began tracking what he ate, and the passage cannot separate the effects of the chart and his diet.

q: What does paragraph 3 of the burn first aid passage suggest about removing rings near a burn?
o: Rings can carry germs that cause burn infections.
Rings hold in heat and make the burn deeper later.
Rings should be cut off if they fit snugly at first.
Waiting to remove them can make removal much harder.
w: Burned skin swells quickly, and an item that slides off easily now 'may have to be cut off an hour later.' The paragraph implies that delay makes removal harder.

n.0: Unsupported: germs are discussed in paragraph 4 in connection with blisters and home remedies, not rings.
n.1: Distortion: paragraph 4 says butter, oil and toothpaste hold in heat; rings are removed because of swelling.
n.2: Distortion: the paragraph says to take items off gently now; cutting is what may be needed if removal waits.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by paragraphs 2 and 4 of the burn first aid passage?
o: The colder the water used on a burn, the faster the burn will heal.
Burns that form blisters should be seen by a doctor without delay.
Some well-meant home remedies can make a minor burn worse than before.
Most burns that happen at home become infected without a bandage.
w: Paragraph 2 says ice can damage already injured tissue, and paragraph 4 says butter, oil and toothpaste hold in heat and may carry bacteria. Together they support the conclusion that some common remedies can worsen a minor burn.

n.0: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says to use cool, not cold, water and warns that extreme cold can damage tissue.
n.1: Contradicts the passage: small blisters are a normal part of a minor burn and are to be left alone; prompt care is for the warning signs in paragraph 5.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage says to watch for infection, but it gives no rate of infection for uncovered burns.

q: Why does the author of the burn first aid passage explain what extreme cold does to blood vessels in the skin?
o: To describe how the body heals a burn over three weeks
To give a reason for the warning against using ice
To show that cold water speeds the healing of a burn
To explain why burned skin swells within an hour
w: The explanation follows the instruction 'Do not use ice or ice water' and tells readers why: extreme cold narrows skin blood vessels and can damage injured tissue.

n.0: Healing time is mentioned in paragraph 1; the explanation in paragraph 2 is about why ice is harmful.
n.2: Reversal: the explanation warns against extreme cold rather than praising it.
n.3: Swelling is explained in paragraph 3 to support removing tight items; it is not linked to cold.

q: What can be inferred from paragraphs 1 and 2 about how newborns were assessed before Apgar's score?
o: Most newborns who struggled to breathe at birth did not survive their first hour of life.
Doctors refused to examine newborns until the mother was out of danger after the birth.
Two staff members could judge one newborn differently, with no shared measure.
Staff relied on special equipment that most hospitals could not afford.
w: Paragraph 1 says there was "no shared, quick method" for judging newborns, and paragraph 2 says staff used vague terms such as "fine" or "a little weak." Without a shared standard, two people could describe the same baby differently and have no common measure to settle it.

n.0: Overstatement: the passage says struggling babies could go unnoticed, but it gives no survival figures.
n.1: "Refused" goes beyond the passage, which says only that staff focused on the mother.
n.3: Paragraph 3 says Apgar's score needed no special equipment; nothing suggests that earlier methods depended on costly devices.

q: What is the most likely reason the author included paragraph 4 in the passage about the Apgar score?
o: To clarify the limits of the score's purpose and note a wider benefit
To argue that the score should be used to predict later development
To describe the five signs checked by the person attending the birth
To show that later doctors found serious flaws in Apgar's method
w: Paragraph 4 first states what the score was not designed to do and what its narrower purpose was, then explains its added value for research. Its job in the passage is to set limits and add a broader effect.

n.1: Paragraph 4 says the opposite: medical groups caution against using the score to predict long-term health.
n.2: Wrong paragraph: the five signs are listed in paragraph 2.
n.3: The caution in paragraph 4 is about misusing the score for prediction, not about a flaw found in Apgar's method.

q: Which title best fits the passage about nighttime noise on a hospital unit?
o: Why Patients Sleep Poorly in Hospitals
Quieting the Night on One Hospital Unit
How One Unit Cut Sleep Medication Requests
Proof That Quiet Hours Speed Patient Recovery
w: The passage describes one unit's noise problem, its quiet-hours program, the results and the team's caution about them. A title naming the unit's effort to quiet its nights covers all five paragraphs.

n.0: Too narrow: the general problem of hospital sleep is only the introduction in paragraph 1.
n.2: Too narrow: the drop in sleep medication requests is one result reported in paragraph 4.
n.3: Overstatement: paragraph 5 says the survey was not a controlled experiment, and recovery was never measured.

q: According to the passage, what share of patients rated their sleep as poor or very poor after quiet hours began?
o: 61 percent
24 percent
49 percent
37 percent
w: Paragraph 4: "The share of patients rating their sleep as poor or very poor fell to 37 percent."

n.0: 61 percent is the share before quiet hours began (paragraph 2).
n.1: 24 is the size of the drop in percentage points (61 minus 37), not the share after the change.
n.2: 49 is the average nighttime noise level in decibels after the change, not a share of patients.

q: Based on paragraph 5, the team most likely plans to repeat its measurements on two other units because it
o: has concluded that the family lounge caused most of the change
found that its first measurements were recorded incorrectly
wants to learn whether similar results appear beyond one unit
expects the other units to be quieter than the first unit was
w: Paragraph 5 lists reasons the first results are uncertain (no controlled design, different patients, the new lounge) and then says the team will measure two more units. Gathering results from more units is the step that addresses those doubts.

n.0: Overreach: the lounge is named as one possible influence, not as the cause of most of the change.
n.1: Nothing in the passage questions the accuracy of the sound meters or the survey records.
n.3: The passage gives no information about noise levels on the other units.

q: Which conclusion about the quiet-hours program is best supported by the information in the passage?
o: It helped patients on the unit recover from their illnesses more quickly than before.
It lowered nighttime noise to a level at which most patients on the unit slept well.
It showed, through fewer medication requests, that patients needed less pain relief.
Noise and poor sleep ratings fell after it began, though other factors may have helped.
w: Paragraph 4 reports lower noise, fewer poor sleep ratings and fewer medication requests. Paragraph 5 notes that the survey was not controlled, the patients differed and a family lounge opened in the same months. The supported conclusion reports the improvement while allowing that other factors may have contributed.

n.0: Recovery was never measured; paragraph 1 says only that poor sleep may slow recovery.
n.1: Misreads the numbers: 37 percent still rated their sleep poor or very poor, and a rating that is not poor is not the same as sleeping well.
n.2: The passage reports requests for sleep medication, not pain relief; linking the two goes beyond the evidence.

q: Which statement based on the passage about quiet hours expresses an opinion rather than a fact?
o: On the morning survey, 61 percent of patients rated their sleep as poor or very poor.
Quiet hours were the most worthwhile change the staff had made in years.
The survey was not designed by the team as a controlled experiment.
Peaks above 80 decibels occurred several times each night.
w: "Most worthwhile" is a judgment that others could reasonably dispute and that no measurement can prove. It is the nurse manager's opinion, reported in paragraph 5.

n.0: The statement contains the words "poor" and "very poor," but it reports what the survey found, which can be checked against the survey records.
n.2: Whether a survey was designed as a controlled experiment can be verified from how it was set up.
n.3: Noise peaks were recorded by sound meters, so this statement can be checked.

q: What does the passage imply about the 6-point drop reported in paragraph 3?
o: It describes only those who stayed, who may differ from those who left.
It shows that each of the 240 enrolled adults lowered their pressure.
It would have been larger if the 68 who left had been measured.
It came from the walks rather than from changes in salt or medicine.
w: Paragraph 3 limits the 6-point figure to "those who finished" and says the 68 who left "were not measured again." Paragraph 5's plan to measure everyone who leaves confirms the gap. The figure may not represent everyone who enrolled.

n.1: Overreach: the figure is an average for the 172 finishers; the 68 who left were not measured.
n.2: Unsupported: the passage gives no basis for guessing whether the missing results were better or worse.
n.3: The passage does not say whether participants changed their diet or medication, so this cannot be inferred.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by the center's plan to track a comparison group next spring?
o: This year's readings were taken incorrectly and will need to be repeated next spring.
The walks had no real effect on blood pressure, and the center expects to show this.
This year's drop cannot be firmly credited to the walks without a group to compare it with.
Adults on the waiting list will probably reach lower readings than adults who walk.
w: A comparison group of adults who are not yet walking shows what happens without the program. Planning one implies that this year's results, which had no such group, cannot by themselves show that the walks caused the drop.

n.0: Nothing in the passage questions how the nurse took the readings.
n.1: Overreach in the other direction: the passage reports a drop among finishers and gives no sign the center doubts the program.
n.3: The passage makes no prediction about the comparison group's readings.

q: A person has stomach cramps after a large milkshake but no trouble after a splash of milk in coffee. What can be inferred from the passage about this pattern?
o: It shows a milk allergy in its mildest early stage.
It is more typical of an intolerance than an allergy.
It means the person's body makes no lactase enzyme.
It calls for carrying an epinephrine auto-injector.
w: Paragraph 3 says intolerance symptoms "often depend on the amount eaten," while paragraph 2 says "even a trace amount" can set off an allergic reaction. Symptoms that appear only with a large amount fit an intolerance better.

n.0: Unsupported: the passage describes no stages of allergy, and allergies can react to trace amounts.
n.2: Paragraph 3 says people with lactose intolerance make "too little" lactase, and the pattern alone does not prove which problem the person has.
n.3: Auto-injectors are mentioned for some people with food allergies; this pattern fits intolerance better.

q: Which conclusion about telling a food allergy from a food intolerance is best supported by the passage?
o: People with an intolerance should avoid problem foods completely to stay safe.
Vomiting after eating is a reliable sign that a person has a food allergy.
Most people who say they are allergic to a food actually have an intolerance.
Testing may be needed, because some symptoms can occur with either condition.
w: Paragraph 5 says vomiting or stomach pain "can occur with either" and advises seeing a provider who "can order tests." The supported conclusion is that symptoms alone may not settle the question.

n.0: Paragraph 4 gives complete avoidance as the usual advice for an allergy; people with an intolerance may only need to limit portions.
n.1: Contradicts paragraph 5, which says vomiting can occur with either condition.
n.2: Overgeneralization: paragraph 1 says people often use "allergic" loosely, but gives no figures on how many are wrong.

q: Which inference about the doses described in paragraph 4 is best supported by the passage?
o: Doses from a unit that was out of range have lost all of their strength.
Doses from a unit that was out of range may sometimes still be usable.
Clinic staff can judge the safety of affected doses by looking at them.
Manufacturers will replace any doses that were stored out of range.
w: Paragraph 4 says the manufacturer or health department "decides whether the doses can still be given," and staff keep them in proper storage meanwhile. That process would be pointless unless some affected doses can still be used.

n.0: Overstatement: if every affected dose were ruined, there would be no decision to make about using them.
n.2: Contradicts paragraph 3: damaged vaccines often look exactly like properly stored ones.
n.3: Not supported: the passage says the manufacturer may be contacted, not that it replaces doses.

q: Which conclusion about a clinic that keeps its vaccines in a small dormitory-style refrigerator is best supported?
o: Its doses face a greater risk of temperature damage that staff cannot see.
Its vaccines will freeze and be ruined within a few days of delivery.
Its staff can keep doses safe by checking their appearance each day.
Its patients are likely to become sick from the vaccines they receive.
w: Paragraph 5 says such units have wide temperature swings and can freeze vaccines near the vent, and paragraph 3 says damaged vaccines often look normal. Together these support a greater, hidden risk of damage.

n.1: Overstatement: the passage says these units can freeze vaccines placed near the vent, not that every vaccine will be ruined in days.
n.2: Contradicts paragraph 3, which says damage often cannot be seen.
n.3: Not supported: paragraph 1 says a damaged vaccine may fail to protect, not that it makes people sick.

q: Which statement based on the passage about storing vaccines expresses an opinion?
o: Many vaccines lose strength when they become too warm.
A few vaccines must be stored frozen rather than refrigerated.
Every clinic should invest in a storage unit built for the purpose.
Staff review the data logger readings at least once each workday.
w: "Should invest" states what the author believes clinics ought to do. Others could reasonably disagree, and no record can prove it true or false, so it is an opinion.

n.0: How a vaccine responds to heat can be measured in testing, so this is a factual claim.
n.1: Storage requirements for vaccines can be verified from manufacturers' directions, so this is a fact.
n.3: How often staff review readings can be verified from clinic records, so this is a fact.

q: What is the main idea of the passage about organ donor registration?
o: Thousands of people in the United States die each year while waiting for a transplant.
Adults should register as organ donors because the need is urgent and common fears are mistaken.
Modern transplant surgery can save the lives of many patients with failing organs.
Because so few deaths allow donation, most registered donors do not end up donating an organ.
w: Every paragraph serves one argument: the need is great (1), registering is easy and matters (2), the usual fears are unfounded (3), registering spares families a hard choice (4), and readers should sign up now (5).

n.0: Too narrow: the waiting-list deaths in paragraph 1 are evidence for the argument, not the argument itself.
n.2: Too broad: the passage is not about what transplant surgery can do but about why readers should register.
n.3: A possible inference from one statistic in paragraph 2, and the author uses that statistic to show why registering matters, not to make this point.

q: Which statement can be inferred from paragraph 4 of the passage about organ donor registration?
o: Some organs that could have been donated are not, because the person's wishes were unknown.
Most people who die without registering would not have wanted to donate their organs.
Families who are asked to decide about donation usually agree to donate.
Relatives often overrule the choice of a person who has joined the donor registry.
w: Paragraph 4 says many relatives say no "simply because they are unsure what their loved one would have wanted." If they refuse out of uncertainty, some of those loved ones would have wanted to donate, so some usable organs go undonated.

n.1: The paragraph says relatives are unsure of the person's wishes, not that the person was against donating.
n.2: The paragraph says many families say no and gives no overall rate, so a claim that most agree is unsupported.
n.3: Reversal: the paragraph says a registry entry answers the question in advance; nothing says relatives overrule it.

q: Based on the passage, with which statement about organ donation would the author most likely agree?
o: Registration matters less than it seems, since so few deaths allow donation.
Families should be asked to approve donation even when a person has registered.
People with serious health problems should still consider registering as donors.
Registered donors may get less aggressive care, but the benefit to others is worth it.
w: Paragraph 3 answers the worry about being "too sick to qualify" by saying doctors decide at the time of death which organs can be used. The author would therefore urge people with health problems to register rather than rule themselves out.

n.0: Reversal: paragraph 2 uses the rarity of donation to argue that registration matters more, not less.
n.1: Paragraph 4 says a name on the registry answers the family's question in advance, so the author sees registration as settling the matter.
n.3: The author denies the premise: paragraph 3 says the treating doctors are separate from the transplant team and donation is considered only after every effort has failed.

q: What is the author's primary purpose in the passage about organ donor registration?
o: To inform readers about the shortage of organs available for transplant
To persuade readers to register as organ donors and tell their families
To correct common myths about who is able to become an organ donor
To explain how families decide whether to donate a relative's organs
w: The author states a position, supports it with reasons and evidence, answers objections, and ends with a direct call to action ("take a few minutes this week to do it, and then tell the people closest to you"). The purpose is to persuade.

n.0: The shortage figures in paragraph 1 support the argument; informing readers about them is not the goal of the whole passage.
n.2: Too narrow: correcting mistaken beliefs is the job of paragraph 3, one step in the larger argument.
n.3: Too narrow: paragraph 4 mentions the family's decision only to show one more reason to register.

q: Which statement from the passage about organ donor registration is a fact rather than an opinion?
o: These fears are understandable, and they deserve a careful answer.
Few decisions ask so little of us and offer so much to strangers.
Seventeen deaths a day is a toll no caring society should accept.
There is no upper age limit for registering.
w: Whether registries set a maximum age can be checked against registry rules, so this statement can be proven true or false: it is a fact.

n.0: "Understandable" and "deserve" are the author's judgments about the fears; they cannot be proven.
n.1: Whether a decision asks "little" and offers "much" is the author's evaluation, which others could dispute.
n.2: The number can be checked, but "a toll no caring society should accept" is a value judgment, so the sentence states an opinion.

q: What does paragraph 1 suggest by saying a health care provider or pharmacist can show which spacer fits an inhaler?
o: Not every spacer is designed to fit every inhaler.
Spacers can be obtained with a prescription from a provider.
Pharmacists teach inhaler use better than other providers.
Each brand of inhaler is sold with a matching spacer.
w: If any spacer fit any inhaler, there would be no need for someone to show which one fits. The sentence implies that spacers and inhalers must be matched.

n.1: The passage says nothing about how spacers are obtained or whether a prescription is needed.
n.2: The sentence names both providers and pharmacists equally; it does not compare them.
n.3: If a matching spacer came with each inhaler, the reader would not need to ask which spacer fits.

q: Why does the author explain in paragraph 1 how a spacer holds a puff of medicine?
o: To persuade readers to buy a particular brand of spacer
To warn that inhalers used alone can cause mouth infection
To describe how metered-dose inhalers are manufactured
To show the benefit that makes the steps that follow worthwhile
w: Paragraph 1 explains the problem (medicine landing in the mouth and throat) and how a spacer solves it, then introduces "the steps below." The explanation gives the reader a reason to follow the procedure.

n.0: No brand is named; the passage advises asking a provider which spacer fits.
n.1: Wrong paragraph and wrong cause: thrush is mentioned in paragraph 4 in connection with steroid medicine.
n.2: The paragraph describes what a spacer does, not how inhalers are made.

q: Based on paragraphs 3 and 4, which change in a person being treated for heat exhaustion would most strongly suggest that the condition has become heat stroke?
o: The person keeps sweating heavily and says he still feels dizzy.
The person's skin feels damp when the nurse touches his forehead.
The person, alert until now, becomes confused about where he is.
The person feels nauseated and asks to lie down in the shade.
w: Paragraph 4 says the person with heat exhaustion generally remains alert, while someone with heat stroke may become confused. A shift from alert to confused is the sign the passage ties to heat stroke and not to heat exhaustion.

n.0: Heavy sweating and dizziness are signs of heat exhaustion (paragraph 3), so they do not point to a change.
n.1: Paragraph 4 says heat stroke skin can be dry or damp, and heat exhaustion skin is clammy, so damp skin does not separate the two.
n.3: Nausea is listed as a sign of heat exhaustion (paragraph 3), not of the change to heat stroke.

q: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 of the passage about lead in older homes about painted windows that are opened and closed often?
o: Their movement lets fresh air carry lead dust safely outdoors.
Their frames contain more lead than any other painted surface.
They should be replaced before a young child moves into the home.
Their frames may shed more lead dust than walls that are left alone.
w: Paragraph 2 says paint releases dust when it wears down, "especially on surfaces that rub together, such as window frames." Windows that are used often rub more, so they are likely to release more dust than untouched walls.

n.0: Not supported: the passage says the dust settles on floors and windowsills.
n.1: Overstatement: the passage says these surfaces wear and release dust, not that they hold more lead.
n.2: Advice the passage never gives; paragraph 4 recommends cleaning and repair.

q: Which inference about patients aged 65 and older is best supported by the passage about Eastside Family Clinic?
o: They missed more visits than younger patients before the texts began.
They will keep more appointments once phone calls replace the texts.
Many of them may never have seen the reminders sent to their phones.
They do not own phones that are able to receive text messages.
w: Paragraph 4 says many patients in this group rarely read text messages and that their no-show rate barely changed. It follows that many of them may not have seen the reminders. The passage supports that much and no more.

n.0: Not supported: the passage gives no no-show rate by age before the program.
n.1: Overreach: the clinic is testing phone calls; the passage does not say how well they will work.
n.3: Overreach: the survey says they rarely read texts, not that their phones cannot receive them.

q: Which inference about the eight schools without a full-time nurse is best supported by paragraph 2?
o: Their students have fewer long-term health conditions than students elsewhere.
Their traveling nurses are less qualified than the nurses at the other schools.
Their principals have asked the board to hire nurses for their buildings.
A child there may need care at a time when no nurse is in the building.
w: Paragraph 2 says the eight schools share two traveling nurses, so a nurse may be twenty minutes or more away when a child needs one. It follows that a child may need care while no nurse is present.

n.0: A possible reason for how nurses are assigned, but the passage gives district-wide totals, not figures for these schools.
n.1: Not supported: the passage says nothing about the nurses' training.
n.2: Not supported: the passage names no requests from principals.

q: Based on paragraph 4 of the passage about school nurses, which conclusion would the author most likely agree with?
o: Hiring nurses costs money, but going without them also costs money and class time.
The district should hire all eight nurses next year, even if other programs must be cut.
Substitute teachers cost the district more each year than a full-time nurse does.
Board members who object to the cost care less about students than about budgets.
w: The author concedes that "the cost is real" but argues that the district already pays for substitutes and pays "in lost learning" when students are sent home. The conclusion that both choices have costs combines those points.

n.1: Contradicts the phased plan in paragraph 4: three nurses next year and the rest over two more years.
n.2: Not supported: the passage gives the cost of a nurse but no yearly figure for substitutes, so no comparison is possible.
n.3: Not supported: the author answers the board members' argument and concedes their point about cost without questioning their motives.

q: A reader takes her blood pressure ten minutes after finishing a cup of coffee. The reading is above her provider's goal but below 180/120. Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: She should call her provider's office today, because the reading is above her goal.
She should call 911, since caffeine can push blood pressure to a dangerous level.
Her monitor is probably faulty and should be checked before she uses it again.
The reading may not reflect her usual pressure, so it should be repeated correctly.
w: Paragraph 2 says to avoid caffeine for at least 30 minutes before measuring, and paragraph 5 says one high reading is not usually a cause for alarm. Together they support treating this reading as unreliable and repeating it under the right conditions.

n.0: Paragraph 5 says to call when readings stay above the goal for several days, not after one reading.
n.1: Overreach: 911 is for readings above 180/120 that stay high along with symptoms; this reading is below that level.
n.2: Not supported: the passage points to the coffee, not the device, as the likely problem.

q: According to the passage about Eastside Family Clinic, what happened to Westside's no-show rate while Eastside was sending texts?
o: It fell from 18 percent to 11 percent.
It stayed near 17 percent throughout.
It rose to 18 percent without the texts.
It fell from 17 percent to 15 percent.
w: Paragraph 3: Westside, which sent no texts, saw its no-show rate drop "from 17 percent to 15 percent."

n.0: Those are Eastside's figures (paragraphs 1 and 2), not Westside's.
n.1: 17 percent is Westside's starting rate; the passage says the rate dropped.
n.2: 18 percent is Eastside's 2023 rate; Westside's rate fell rather than rose.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by the comparison of the two clinics in paragraph 3 of the passage about Eastside Family Clinic?
o: The texts caused all of Eastside's drop from 18 percent to 11 percent.
Longer evening hours, not the texts, explain Eastside's improvement.
The texts will cut Westside's no-show rate by 7 points when they begin.
The texts likely helped, but they account for less than the full 7-point drop.
w: Eastside fell 7 points (18 to 11 percent) while Westside, without texts, fell 2 points (17 to 15 percent), possibly because of the shared evening hours. The comparison suggests the texts added to an improvement that was partly happening anyway.

n.0: Ignores Westside's 2-point drop without texts, which shows that something else explains part of Eastside's drop.
n.1: Goes too far: Eastside fell much more than Westside, and paragraph 3 says the texts likely made a difference beyond the shared change.
n.2: Overgeneralizes: paragraph 5 says Westside's results will show whether its patients respond the same way; the outcome is not known.

q: A person uses about a quarter teaspoon of iodized salt a day and eats no other iodine sources. Based on the passage about iodized salt, which conclusion is best supported?
o: The person meets an adult's daily need of about 150 micrograms.
The person will develop a goiter within a few months.
The person likely gets about half of an adult's daily iodine need.
The person gets about 220 micrograms, enough for pregnancy.
w: Paragraph 4: a quarter teaspoon of iodized salt supplies roughly half of an adult's daily need of about 150 micrograms, so with no other sources the person gets roughly 75 micrograms.

n.0: Misreads the figures: about 150 micrograms is the whole daily need, and a quarter teaspoon supplies roughly half of it.
n.1: Overreach: falling short of the daily need does not show a goiter will form, let alone on a set timeline.
n.3: Misreads the figures: 220 micrograms is the pregnancy need, far more than a quarter teaspoon supplies.

q: What is the author's primary purpose in the passage about school nurses?
o: To inform readers how many district students have asthma, diabetes or severe allergies
To praise the school secretary who helped a wheezing second grader recover
To persuade readers to support placing a nurse in every school in the district
To explain the range of duties a school nurse carries out during a school day
w: The author makes a claim (every school needs a nurse), supports it with an anecdote, numbers and a cost argument, answers an objection, and ends with a call to action: "I urge every parent...to attend that meeting or write to the board." That is persuasion.

n.0: The statistics in paragraph 2 are evidence for the argument; informing readers of them is not the purpose of the whole passage.
n.1: The secretary is thanked in paragraph 1, but the story is used to show that she should not have been the most qualified person present.
n.3: Paragraph 3 lists duties to support the argument; it is one part, not the purpose of the whole passage.

q: Why does the author most likely mention in paragraph 1 that X-rays, safe transfusions and antibiotics were not yet available?
o: To explain why Cornish needed several weeks to recover in the hospital
To show how great a risk Williams took by operating inside the chest
To suggest that Williams later helped develop these medical tools
To compare surgery in Chicago with surgery in other cities of the time
w: The detail sits between "such operations [were] deadly" and "chose with remarkable courage to operate anyway": it shows how few tools surgeons had, and so how risky the operation was.

n.0: The passage does not connect these missing tools to the length of Cornish's recovery.
n.2: Not supported: the passage never says Williams worked on any of these tools.
n.3: No other city is mentioned; the detail describes surgery in general at the time.

q: Which statement based on the passage about Eastside Family Clinic expresses an opinion rather than a fact?
o: The texting service costs the clinic about $400 a month.
The texting program is the best money the clinic has spent.
Westside sent no reminder texts during the first half of 2024.
About 18 percent of Eastside's 2023 visits were missed without notice.
w: "The best money we have ever spent" is the director's judgment of the program's value; other staff are more cautious, which shows that reasonable people can disagree with it.

n.0: A cost that billing records could confirm, so it is a fact.
n.2: A verifiable statement about what Westside did.
n.3: A figure from clinic records that can be checked.

q: Which statement from the passage about school nurses expresses an opinion?
o: Our children deserve a nurse down the hall, not across town.
This year, district records list 214 students with asthma.
The other eight share two nurses who travel between buildings.
Last spring, a second grader at Lincoln Elementary began wheezing during recess.
w: "Deserve" expresses a value judgment about what children should have; it cannot be proven true or false, and others could reasonably disagree.

n.1: A number from district records that can be checked, so it is a fact.
n.2: A verifiable statement about how nurses are assigned.
n.3: An event that witnesses and school records could confirm.

q: Which statement from the home blood pressure instructions expresses an opinion rather than a fact?
o: Few habits give you and your provider more useful information for less effort.
Home readings show how your pressure behaves during ordinary life, outside a clinic.
A full bladder can raise your blood pressure reading.
Some monitor models erase their stored readings when the batteries are changed.
w: The writers introduce this sentence with "In our view," and it judges the value of a habit compared with others; it cannot be measured or proven, so it is an opinion.

n.1: A factual claim about what home readings capture; it can be checked.
n.2: A factual claim about a measurable effect; it can be tested.
n.3: A factual claim about how some devices work; it can be verified.

q: Which title best fits the passage about Eastside Family Clinic?
o: How Evening Hours Cut Missed Appointments
Text Reminders and Missed Visits: Early Results
Why Older Patients Prefer Phone Reminders
How Text Messages Ended Missed Appointments
w: The passage describes the texting program and the drop in no-shows (paragraph 2), weighs how much of the drop the texts explain (paragraph 3), notes a group they did not help (paragraph 4) and stresses that the results are early and limited (paragraph 5). The title names that topic and its tentative main idea.

n.0: Paragraph 3 offers evening hours as a possible reason for part of the drop at both clinics; the passage is mainly about the texts.
n.2: Too narrow and overstated: older patients appear in paragraph 4, and the passage does not say they prefer calls; the clinic is only testing them.
n.3: Overstatement: no-shows fell to 11 percent; they did not end.

q: What does paragraph 5 of the passage about iodized salt suggest about a person who avoids iodized salt but eats plenty of dairy products and seafood?
o: The person may still get enough iodine from these other foods.
The person is likely to develop a goiter within a few years.
The person needs about 220 micrograms of iodine each day.
The person should switch to sea salt to add iodine to the diet.
w: Paragraph 5 calls dairy products, eggs and seafood "other good sources" of iodine and warns about people who eat few of them. It suggests that someone who eats plenty of them may meet the need without iodized salt.

n.1: Overreach: the passage gives no reason to expect goiter in someone eating good iodine sources.
n.2: Wrong group: 220 micrograms is the figure for pregnant women, and nothing says this person is pregnant.
n.3: Contradicts paragraph 5: sea salt usually contains little or no added iodine.

q: Which title best fits the passage about Daniel Hale Williams?
o: Daniel Hale Williams and the History of Heart Surgery
Daniel Hale Williams's Years at Freedmen's Hospital
Pioneers Who Opened Medicine to Everyone
Daniel Hale Williams: Surgeon and Builder of Institutions
w: The passage presents a daring 1893 operation (1), Williams's path into medicine (2), and the hospitals, training programs and professional groups he founded or led (3-5), ending with the claim that these may be his most lasting gift. The title names both sides of that main idea.

n.0: Off center: the passage describes one operation, not the history of heart surgery.
n.1: Too narrow: Freedmen's Hospital is one detail in paragraph 4.
n.2: Too broad: the passage is about one physician, and this title would fit a whole book.

q: What does paragraph 1 suggest about blood pressure readings taken in a clinic?
o: They are usually lower than the readings people take at home.
For some people, they may run higher than everyday pressure.
They are no longer needed once home monitoring has begun.
They are less accurate because clinic equipment is older.
w: Paragraph 1 says home readings show pressure "away from the stress some people feel in a clinic." Since the passage says stress can affect readings, it implies that for some people clinic readings may be higher than their everyday pressure.

n.0: Reverses the implication: stress in the clinic would push readings up, not down.
n.2: Contradicts paragraph 1, which tells the reader to bring the home record to each appointment.
n.3: Not supported: the passage blames stress, not equipment.

q: Which inference about noise-related tinnitus is best supported by paragraphs 1 and 2?
o: It results from reduced activity in the brain's hearing centers.
It can last because the damaged hair cells are not replaced.
It usually fades once the hair cells have had time to regrow.
It starts when the cochlea sends stronger signals to the brain.
w: Paragraph 2 says noise breaks hair cells and "they do not grow back," and paragraph 1 says for some people the ringing lingers or never leaves. Together they support the inference that the condition can be lasting because the damage is permanent.

n.0: Reversal: paragraph 2 says the hearing centers "may become more active," not less.
n.2: Contradicts paragraph 2: the hair cells do not grow back.
n.3: Reversal: paragraph 2 says fewer signals arrive from the ear.

q: Based on paragraph 3, which person would most likely be at greater risk of forming a kidney stone?
o: A clerk who replaces her salty snacks with fresh fruit at lunchtime
A roofer who works outdoors through a hot week without extra fluids
A teacher who drinks enough water each day to keep her urine pale
A retired driver who adds a glass of milk to each of his meals
w: Paragraph 3 says stones form more readily when people take in too little water and lose more water through sweat in hot weather. A roofer working in heat without extra fluids fits both risks.

n.0: Opposite: paragraph 3 says high-salt diets raise the risk, so cutting salt would lower it.
n.2: Opposite: paragraph 4 gives pale yellow urine as the goal of preventive advice.
n.3: Opposite: paragraph 4 says calcium eaten with meals binds oxalate, so less reaches the kidneys.

q: Based on paragraph 4 of the passage about the hospital fall-prevention program, which inference is best supported?
o: Falls that caused an injury fell by more than half.
More patients were getting help before they left their beds.
High-risk patients stopped trying to leave their beds at night.
Most of the falls that still occurred took place during the day.
w: Staff reported fewer calls for help that came after a patient was already out of bed. With hourly rounds and bed alarms, this suggests patients were more often assisted before they got up.

n.0: A miscalculation: a drop from 19 to 11 is a fall of 8, about 42 percent, which is less than half.
n.2: Overreach: fewer late calls for help does not show that patients stopped getting up.
n.3: Not supported: the passage gives no breakdown of when the remaining falls happened.

q: Based on paragraph 3 of the passage about street trees and shade, which inference is best supported?
o: Most residents of the northern neighborhoods have air conditioning.
Heat-related deaths are higher in the eastern districts than in the north.
Eastern residents are more exposed to sun-heated pavement than northern ones.
The parks department planted more trees in the north after the 2023 survey.
w: The survey shows tree canopy covering 38 percent of northern land but 11 percent of eastern land, and paragraph 2 says unshaded surfaces are hotter. Eastern residents therefore walk on more sun-heated pavement.

n.0: Unsupported: the passage says more eastern residents lack air conditioning, which says nothing definite about most northern residents.
n.1: Overreach: plausible, but the passage gives no figures on deaths by district.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage describes the survey's findings, not any planting that followed.

q: Which conclusion about calcium in the diet is best supported by paragraph 4?
o: Calcium in food is the main ingredient of most stones, so it should be kept to a minimum.
Eating calcium-rich foods will dissolve stones that have already formed in the kidney.
For many people with past stones, keeping calcium-rich foods at meals may help prevent new ones.
Calcium binds to oxalate in the kidneys, which keeps crystals from forming there.
w: Paragraph 4 says calcium eaten with meals binds oxalate in the digestive tract, so less reaches the kidneys, and that cutting calcium can raise the risk for many people.

n.0: Contradicts paragraph 4: patients are not told to cut calcium, and cutting it can raise the risk.
n.1: Not supported: the passage says nothing about dissolving existing stones.
n.3: Wrong location: the binding happens in the digestive tract, before oxalate reaches the kidneys.

q: With which statement would the author of the passage about street trees and shade most likely agree?
o: Cooling centers should be closed so that their funds can pay for trees.
Cooling centers are useful but do not replace shade along city streets.
Tree planting should wait until better drought-tolerant species exist.
Sidewalk damage is a good reason to limit trees in the eastern districts.
w: Paragraph 1 says the current steps "save lives," and paragraph 4 says cooling centers help those who can reach them while shade protects everyone on the block.

n.0: Overreach: the author values cooling centers and argues for adding shade, not for closing them.
n.2: Contradicts paragraphs 4 and 5: drought-tolerant species are already a solution, and the author urges planting now.
n.3: Opposite: the author answers the sidewalk concern with wider planting beds and still calls for planting.

q: Which conclusion about antivenom supply is best supported by paragraph 5?
o: Snakebite deaths have risen since 2017 as a result of the WHO listing.
Snakebite is a serious problem in every country that has venomous snakes.
Antivenom shortages are linked in part to the poor economics of producing it.
Shortages could be solved by switching to freeze-dried products.
w: Paragraph 5 says antivenom is costly to produce and sold in small amounts, that some manufacturers stopped making it, and that shortages followed: the business costs are part of the cause.

n.0: False cause: the passage gives no figures on deaths after 2017 and does not link the WHO listing to any change in them.
n.1: Overgeneralization: the passage names parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America.
n.3: Unsupported: freeze-drying is about storage (paragraph 3), not cost or supply.

q: Which conclusion about the hospital fall-prevention program is best supported by the passage?
o: The bed alarms were responsible for most of the 31 percent decline in falls.
Other hospitals that adopt the program will cut their fall rates by about one-third.
The extra night nurses, rather than the program, caused the decline in falls.
The program may have reduced falls, but other changes that year could also explain the drop.
w: Paragraph 4 gives a 31 percent decline after the program, and paragraph 5 names two other changes (more night nurses, slightly younger patients) that could have contributed. The most modest conclusion that uses all the evidence is that the program may have helped.

n.0: Not supported: the passage gives no breakdown of which part of the program, if any, caused the drop.
n.1: Overgeneralization: the results come from one type of ward in one hospital, as the report notes.
n.2: Overreach in the other direction: the report says either change could have contributed, not that the nurses were the cause.

q: According to the passage, what did the county program's follow-up tests show?
o: Levels fell below 2 pCi/L in 141 of the 432 homes with high readings.
Levels fell below 4 pCi/L in 94 percent of the 2,400 tested households.
Levels fell below 2 pCi/L in 141 of the 150 homes with mitigation systems.
Levels in 18 percent of mitigated homes stayed at or above 4 pCi/L.
w: Paragraph 4: "Among the 150 high-reading households that went on to install a mitigation system, follow-up tests found that levels fell below 2 pCi/L in 141 homes."

n.0: Wrong group: 141 is out of the 150 homes that installed systems, not all 432 high-reading homes.
n.1: Wrong group: the follow-up tests covered the 150 mitigated homes, not every household that tested.
n.3: Misplaced number: 18 percent is the share of all tested households with high first readings.

q: Which conclusion is best supported by the county radon program's results?
o: Mitigation systems bring radon below 2 pCi/L in every home that installs one.
Most households in the county have radon levels above the EPA action level.
Homes near a high-radon house should install a system without first testing.
A home's radon level cannot be judged reliably from the readings of nearby homes.
w: Paragraph 4 reports that many high-reading homes sat a few hundred feet from houses with low readings, which supports paragraph 3's point that each home must be tested.

n.0: Overstatement: levels fell below 2 pCi/L in 141 of 150 homes, not all of them.
n.1: Contradicts the data: 18 percent of tested households, not most, were at or above 4 pCi/L.
n.2: Advice the passage does not give; it stresses testing each home.

q: What is the main purpose of paragraph 3 in the passage about donated blood?
o: To persuade readers that blood centers need more equipment
To compare how long each blood product can be stored
To describe the tests performed on each sample tube
To explain how spinning separates blood into its parts
w: Paragraph 3 explains what a centrifuge is and how spinning makes the parts of blood settle into layers by weight before they are bagged separately.

n.0: The paragraph explains a process; it makes no argument or appeal.
n.1: Wrong paragraph: storage times are given in paragraph 4.
n.2: Wrong paragraph: blood typing and infection screening are in paragraph 2.

q: Why does the author most likely begin a sentence in paragraph 4 with the word "Surprisingly"?
o: To signal that the advice runs against what readers might expect
To show that doctors disagree about what causes stones
To introduce a new risk factor that raises the chance of stones
To suggest that the advice about calcium has not been proven
w: Readers might assume calcium-rich foods should be cut because stones contain calcium; "Surprisingly" prepares them for advice that goes the other way, which the next sentences explain.

n.1: Not stated: the paragraph describes what doctors commonly advise, not a disagreement among them.
n.2: Reversal: the sentence explains why keeping calcium may lower the risk, not a new factor that raises it.
n.3: Surprise is not doubt: the author explains the reason for the advice and presents it as sound.

q: What is the author's primary purpose in the passage about street trees and shade?
o: To inform readers about how pavement absorbs and releases heat
To persuade the city to fund tree planting in its hottest areas
To describe the city's heat warnings and cooling centers
To explain why tree roots can damage city sidewalks
w: The author makes a claim (shade is public health infrastructure), supports it with evidence, answers critics and ends with a call for the council to fund planting in the eastern districts now.

n.0: Purpose of one part: the heat facts in paragraph 2 are evidence for the argument, not the purpose of the whole passage.
n.2: Too narrow: these are mentioned in paragraph 1 to set up the argument.
n.3: Too narrow: sidewalk damage is a critic's concern the author answers in paragraph 4.

q: Which statement from the passage about tinnitus is an opinion?
o: Loud noise can bend or break these cells, and they do not grow back.
Tinnitus may be heard in one ear or both.
Certain medications and head injuries can produce tinnitus.
Prevention is by far the wisest approach.
w: "By far the wisest" is a value judgment that cannot be proven and that others could dispute; it is an opinion.

n.0: A fact: physical damage to hair cells can be verified by research.
n.1: A fact: where the sound is heard can be checked by asking and testing patients.
n.2: A fact: a verifiable claim about causes, with no judgment word.

q: Which statement from the passage about the hospital fall-prevention program is an opinion?
o: Falls that caused an injury fell from 19 the year before to 11.
More than half of the previous year's falls happened between midnight and 6 a.m.
The plan is an easy choice for any hospital that takes patient safety seriously.
The hospital added two nurses to the night shift on each medical ward.
w: Calling the plan "an easy choice" and implying that hospitals that do not adopt it do not take safety seriously is a judgment; others could reasonably disagree. A report's view is still an opinion.

n.0: A fact: the counts can be checked against hospital records; numbers alone do not make a statement an opinion, but these carry no judgment.
n.1: A fact: verifiable from the hospital's review of each fall.
n.3: A fact: staffing changes can be confirmed from hospital records.

q: Which sentence from the passage about radon expresses a judgment rather than a verifiable fact?
o: Do-it-yourself test kits are sold at hardware stores and usually cost less than $30.
Given how little a test kit costs, skipping the test is a foolish gamble.
The EPA ranks radon as the second leading cause of lung cancer in the United States.
Installation typically costs about as much as other moderate home repairs.
w: "A foolish gamble" is the author's judgment; others could reasonably disagree, and it cannot be proven.

n.0: A fact: prices and store availability can be checked.
n.2: A fact: what the EPA reports can be verified from its publications.
n.3: A factual claim: typical installation costs can be compared with repair costs.

q: Which statement from the passage about street trees and shade is a fact?
o: Paved streets and rooftops absorb sunlight all day and release it at night.
The city should treat shade as basic public health infrastructure.
These are fair concerns, and each has an answer.
Waiting for the next record-breaking summer would be a costly mistake.
w: How paved surfaces absorb and release heat can be measured and verified; the sentence contains no judgment word.

n.1: An opinion: "should" signals a recommendation others could reject.
n.2: An opinion: calling the critics' concerns 'fair' is the author's judgment.
n.3: An opinion: calling a choice a "costly mistake" is a judgment about the future that cannot be verified.

q: What is the main idea of the passage about donated blood?
o: Platelets are the hardest blood product to keep because they spoil within about a week.
Blood donation is a quick, safe way for a single donor to help as many as three patients.
Testing samples for infections is the most important step in handling donated blood.
Donated blood is labeled, tested and split into parts, each stored in a way that suits it.
w: The passage follows a donation through labeling and testing (paragraph 2), separation (paragraph 3) and storage of each product (paragraphs 4-5). The key covers the whole process.

n.0: Too narrow: platelets' short shelf life is the focus of part of paragraph 4 and paragraph 5 only.
n.1: Off target: paragraph 1 mentions the time and the three patients, but the passage is about what happens to blood after donation, and safety is never discussed.
n.2: Not supported: the passage describes testing as one step and does not rank the steps.

q: The passage implies that a blood center serving many trauma patients most likely depends on
o: a steady flow of recent platelet donations
large frozen reserves of platelets
plasma that can be stored for a year
red cells drawn through a separate process
w: Paragraph 5 says platelets spoil so quickly that centers cannot stockpile them, and that a trauma patient may need platelets from several donors in one night. Such a center must keep receiving fresh platelets.

n.1: Contradicts the passage: platelets are kept at room temperature and cannot be stockpiled; freezing applies to plasma.
n.2: Wrong product: plasma's long storage is stated, but the trauma need described in paragraph 5 is for platelets.
n.3: Wrong product: the separate process in paragraph 5 collects platelets, not red cells.

q: What is the main idea of the passage about antivenom?
o: Albert Calmette produced one of the first antivenoms for cobra bites in what is now Vietnam.
Snakebite deaths would come to an end if more companies chose to manufacture antivenom.
Antivenom is still made with animal antibodies as in the 1890s, but it can be hard to obtain.
Polyvalent antivenoms protect patients against the bite of any snake in the world.
w: The passage traces antivenom's origin (paragraph 1), the method of making it (paragraphs 2-3), its species limits (paragraph 4) and current shortages (paragraph 5).

n.0: Too narrow: this is a detail from paragraph 1 only.
n.1: Overstatement: the passage links stopped production to shortages but never claims more production would end deaths.
n.3: Overstatement: paragraph 4 says a polyvalent product covers the snakes most likely to bite in a given region.

q: The passage suggests that a polyvalent antivenom made for one region
o: contains fewer antibodies than a single-species product
is made by mixing several finished antivenoms together
causes fewer allergic reactions than other antivenoms
may not be effective against snakes common in another region
w: Paragraph 4 says an antivenom works against the venoms it was made from and that a polyvalent product covers the snakes most likely to bite in a given region. Snakes common elsewhere may not be covered.

n.0: Not supported: the passage says nothing about the amount of antibody in each type.
n.1: Wrong process: paragraph 4 says manufacturers combine venoms, not finished products.
n.2: Not supported: reactions are discussed only in connection with purification, not polyvalent products.
